findings.title: Compose service runs privileged
findings.description: ComposeService api runs with `privileged: true`, disabling container isolation entirely. Code execution in this service is equivalent to root on the host.

remediation.summary: Remove privileged; grant specific cap_add entries instead.
remediation.patch:
privileged: false
cap_drop: ["ALL"]
cap_add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]

notes: Directly reachable from the internet.
Holds secret or credential material.

findings.title: Compose service mounts the Docker socket
findings.description: ComposeService api mounts /var/run/docker.sock. This grants full control of the Docker daemon, which is root on the host by another name.

remediation.summary: Use a socket proxy with a minimal API allowlist, or rootless Docker.

notes: Directly reachable from the internet.
Holds secret or credential material.

findings.title: Compose service has plaintext credentials in environment
findings.description: Credential-shaped environment variables are set inline in the compose file, which is version-controlled and visible to anyone who can run `docker inspect`.

evidence.description: credential-like env vars with literal values

remediation.summary: Move values to an untracked env_file or to Docker/Swarm secrets.
remediation.patch:
env_file: [.env]      # add .env to .gitignore
# or, in swarm mode:
# secrets: [db_password]

notes: Directly reachable from the internet.
Holds secret or credential material.

findings.title: Container runs in privileged mode
findings.description: Container shop/web runs with `privileged: true`, which disables essentially every container isolation control: all Linux capabilities are granted, /dev is fully exposed, and AppArmor/seccomp are effectively bypassed. An attacker with code execution in this container can mount the host filesystem, write to /etc/kubernetes, read the kubelet credentials, and take over the node -- and from the node, every other pod scheduled on it.

remediation.summary: Remove privileged mode and grant only the specific capabilities needed.
remediation.guidance: Identify why privilege was needed. The usual culprits are raw sockets (NET_RAW), binding to ports below 1024 (NET_BIND_SERVICE), or device access. Grant those capabilities individually. If the workload genuinely needs host access (CNI plugin, node exporter), isolate it on dedicated nodes with taints and document the exception.
remediation.patch:
securityContext:
  privileged: false
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: []            # add back only what is proven necessary

notes: Reachable from the internet in 3 hops.

findings.title: Container mounts the container runtime socket
findings.description: Deployment shop/storefront mounts the Docker/containerd/CRI-O socket. This is equivalent to granting root on the node: anyone who can write to the socket can start a new privileged container with the host filesystem mounted. There is no meaningful sandbox left.

evidence.description: hostPath volume includes the runtime socket

remediation.summary: Remove the socket mount; use a rootless build tool or a proxy with an allowlist.
remediation.guidance: For image builds use Kaniko, Buildah rootless, or BuildKit with the rootless daemon. For log/metric collection use the kubelet API or the CRI API through a dedicated read-only proxy such as docker-socket-proxy with the API surface restricted to what the agent actually needs.
remediation.patch:
# delete this volume and its volumeMount
# - name: docker-sock
#   hostPath:
#     path: /var/run/docker.sock

notes: Reachable from the internet in 2 hops.

findings.title: Plaintext credential in container environment variables
findings.description: Environment variables DB_PASSWORD, STRIPE_API_KEY on Container shop/web contain literal values and are named like credentials. Env vars are visible to anyone with `kubectl describe pod`, are captured in crash dumps and in most APM/error-tracking agents, are inherited by every child process, and are readable from /proc/<pid>/environ by anything sharing the PID namespace.

evidence.description: env vars with literal values: DB_PASSWORD, STRIPE_API_KEY

remediation.summary: Move the value into a Secret and reference it, or mount it as a file.
remediation.guidance: Files are preferable to env vars: they can be rotated without a pod restart and are not inherited by child processes. Best of all, source from an external secret manager (External Secrets Operator, Vault Agent, cloud CSI driver) so the material never lives in the cluster's etcd at all.
remediation.patch:
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: app-db
        key: password

notes: Reachable from the internet in 3 hops.

findings.title: Ingress does not enforce TLS
findings.description: Ingress shop/storefront-ingress accepts traffic without TLS. Credentials, session cookies, and response data cross the public internet in cleartext, and there is nothing to stop an on-path attacker rewriting responses to serve malicious JavaScript.

evidence.expected: a TLS block with a valid secret

remediation.summary: Add a TLS block and force HTTPS redirection.
remediation.patch:
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: ["app.example.com"]
      secretName: app-tls

notes: Directly reachable from the internet.

findings.title: Service exposes an administrative or database port
findings.description: Service shop/postgres exposes port(s) 5432 and is reachable from outside the cluster. Database, cache, and management ports (5432, 3306, 6379, 9200, 27017, 2375, 10250, 2379...) are routinely scanned; several of these protocols have no authentication enabled by default.

remediation.summary: Make the service ClusterIP and reach it through a bastion, VPN, or port-forward.
remediation.patch:
spec:
  type: ClusterIP     # not NodePort / LoadBalancer

findings.title: Secret material committed to the repository
findings.description: Secret shop/shop-db contains inline `data`/`stringData` in a manifest tracked in version control. base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone with repository read access -- including every CI job, every fork, and the full git history after the value is "removed" -- has these credentials. Rotation is the only remedy once this has been pushed.

remediation.summary: Rotate the credential, then source it from a secret manager.
remediation.guidance: Order of operations matters: rotate first (assume it is compromised), then migrate. Use External Secrets Operator, Vault Agent Injector, Sealed Secrets, or SOPS with a KMS key. Scrub git history with git-filter-repo and force-rotate any credential that was ever pushed.

notes: 4 hops from the internet; requires chaining.
Holds secret or credential material.

findings.title: Container can escalate privileges
findings.description: allowPrivilegeEscalation is not set to false on Container shop/postgres. A setuid binary or a `sudo`-like helper inside the image can gain more privileges than its parent process, which turns a limited RCE into root inside the container and shortens the path to a container escape.

remediation.summary: Set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false.
remediation.patch:
securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

findings.title: Container runs as root
findings.description: Container shop/postgres has no runAsNonRoot/runAsUser constraint, so it runs as UID 0 inside the container. Root in the container means write access to every file in the image, the ability to install tooling at runtime, and a materially easier escape if a kernel or runtime vulnerability is available.

remediation.summary: Run as a dedicated non-root UID.
remediation.guidance: Add a non-root user in the Dockerfile, then enforce it in the manifest. Setting runAsNonRoot alone makes the kubelet refuse to start an image whose USER is root, which surfaces the problem at deploy time rather than at audit time.
remediation.patch:
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  runAsGroup: 10001

notes: Reachable from the internet in 3 hops.

findings.title: Internet-reachable workload has no ingress NetworkPolicy
findings.description: Deployment shop/storefront is reachable from the internet and no NetworkPolicy restricts ingress to it. Kubernetes networking is flat by default, so once an attacker has code execution in any pod in the cluster they can reach this workload directly on its pod IP -- and this workload can reach everything else. Segmentation is the control that turns one compromised pod into one compromised pod rather than a cluster-wide incident.

evidence.description: no NetworkPolicy selects this workload for ingress

remediation.summary: Apply default-deny ingress in the namespace, then allow only required sources.
remediation.patch:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: {{ namespace }}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-ingress-controller
  namespace: {{ namespace }}
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: {app: {{ name }}}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx}
      ports:
        - {protocol: TCP, port: 8080}

notes: Reachable from the internet in 2 hops.

findings.title: LoadBalancer Service has no source IP restriction
findings.description: Service shop/storefront provisions a cloud load balancer with no loadBalancerSourceRanges, so it is reachable from the entire internet. This bypasses the ingress controller and therefore also bypasses any WAF, authentication, or rate limiting configured there.

remediation.summary: Restrict source ranges, or move the workload behind the ingress controller.
remediation.patch:
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 203.0.113.0/24

findings.title: ClusterRole grants full cluster administration
findings.description: ClusterRole shop-operator grants `*` verbs on `*` resources cluster-wide. Any subject bound to it owns the cluster: it can read every Secret in every namespace, create privileged pods on any node, and modify admission webhooks to make the compromise persistent and invisible.

remediation.summary: Replace the wildcard role with an explicitly enumerated least-privilege role.
remediation.guidance: Derive the real permission set from audit logs (`audit2rbac` or the API server audit log filtered by the subject) rather than guessing. Bind cluster-admin only to break-glass identities that are MFA-gated and alerted on.
remediation.patch:
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update"]

findings.title: Compose service publishes a port on all interfaces
findings.description: ComposeService api publishes 8080:8080 without binding to a specific host IP, so the port is reachable on every interface -- including the public one on a cloud VM. Docker also writes iptables rules directly, which commonly bypasses host firewall configuration such as ufw.

remediation.summary: Bind to localhost and front the service with a reverse proxy.

findings.title: Pod shares the host network namespace
findings.description: Deployment shop/storefront runs with hostNetwork: true. The pod shares the node's network namespace, so it can sniff traffic destined for other pods on the node, bind to privileged node ports, bypass NetworkPolicy entirely (policies do not apply to host-network pods), and reach the kubelet on localhost:10250.

remediation.summary: Use the pod network and expose the workload through a Service.
remediation.patch:
spec:
  hostNetwork: false
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst

notes: Reachable from the internet in 2 hops.

findings.title: Pod shares the host PID or IPC namespace
findings.description: Sharing hostPID lets the container see and signal every process on the node, and read secrets from other processes' /proc/<pid>/environ. Sharing hostIPC exposes shared memory segments belonging to other workloads.

remediation.summary: Remove hostPID and hostIPC.
remediation.patch:
spec:
  hostPID: false
  hostIPC: false

notes: Reachable from the internet in 2 hops.

findings.title: Container adds dangerous Linux capabilities
findings.description: Container shop/sidecar-agent adds capabilities SYS_ADMIN, NET_RAW. SYS_ADMIN is close to full root; SYS_PTRACE allows reading memory of other processes; NET_ADMIN permits traffic redirection and ARP spoofing; SYS_MODULE allows loading kernel modules, which is a direct host takeover.

remediation.summary: Drop ALL, then add back only the minimum.
remediation.patch:
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]   # example only

notes: Reachable from the internet in 3 hops.

findings.title: NodePort service exposes the workload on every node
findings.description: A NodePort opens the port on every node in the cluster. Whether that is internet-reachable depends entirely on node security groups, which are usually managed by a different team than the manifest -- so this is exposure you cannot verify from the manifest alone.

remediation.summary: Prefer ClusterIP behind an Ingress; if NodePort is required, restrict node security groups.

findings.title: Object storage bucket has a public ACL
findings.description: aws_s3_bucket assets is configured with a public-read or public-read-write ACL. Public buckets are found by automated scanners within hours. public-read-write is worse than disclosure: anyone can also overwrite objects, which turns the bucket into a malware distribution point under your domain.

remediation.summary: Set the ACL to private and enable the account-level public access block.
remediation.patch:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "this" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.this.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

findings.title: Secret is reachable from an internet-facing workload
findings.description: Secret shop/shop-db is only 4 hops from the internet along the data-flow graph. An RCE in the internet-facing component in that chain yields this secret directly. This is not a misconfiguration on its own -- it is a statement about blast radius that should drive where you invest in detection.

remediation.summary: Shorten the trust chain -- scope the secret, or broker access through a short-lived token.
remediation.guidance: Prefer workload identity (IRSA, Workload Identity, SPIFFE) over long-lived secrets. Where a static secret is unavoidable, scope it to the single consumer and rotate on a schedule short enough that theft has a bounded window.

notes: 4 hops from the internet; requires chaining.
Holds secret or credential material.

findings.title: Secret material in build instructions
findings.description: DockerImage node:latest embeds credential-shaped values in ENV/ARG/RUN. Docker layers are immutable and independently pullable: deleting the value in a later layer does not remove it, and anyone who can pull the image can extract it with `docker history` or by unpacking the layer tarballs.

remediation.summary: Rotate the credential and use BuildKit secret mounts.
remediation.patch:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci --omit=dev

notes: No path from an external entity was found, so remote exploitation requires an existing foothold.
Holds secret or credential material.

findings.title: Container does not drop all capabilities
findings.description: Container shop/postgres keeps the default Docker capability set (CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, SETUID, SETGID, NET_RAW and others). SETUID/SETGID enable local privilege escalation via setuid binaries; NET_RAW enables ARP/DNS spoofing against pods sharing the node network.

remediation.summary: Drop ALL capabilities as the baseline.
remediation.patch:
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]

findings.title: Container root filesystem is writable
findings.description: A writable root filesystem lets an attacker with code execution drop a web shell, overwrite application binaries, or install persistence that survives a process restart. It also removes a cheap tripwire: with a read-only root, most post-exploitation tooling fails immediately and noisily.

remediation.summary: Make the root filesystem read-only and mount emptyDir for writable paths.
remediation.patch:
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
# volumes:
#   - name: tmp
#     emptyDir: {}

findings.title: Container has no CPU or memory limits
findings.description: Without resource limits, Container shop/postgres can consume all allocatable CPU and memory on its node. A memory leak or a deliberately expensive request becomes a node-wide outage: the kubelet begins evicting neighbouring pods, and a single compromised workload becomes a cluster-wide denial of service primitive.

remediation.summary: Set requests and limits; enforce defaults with a LimitRange.

findings.title: Pod does not set a seccomp profile
findings.description: No seccomp profile is applied, so the container may issue all ~350 syscalls. Most container escapes published in the last several years relied on syscalls that RuntimeDefault blocks outright.

findings.title: Workload has no egress NetworkPolicy
findings.description: StatefulSet shop/postgres has unrestricted egress. That is the exfiltration path and the command-and-control path: a compromised pod can reach any external host, any internal service, and the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254 to steal node IAM credentials.

remediation.summary: Default-deny egress; allow DNS plus the specific destinations required.
remediation.patch:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
  namespace: {{ namespace }}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except: ["169.254.169.254/32", "10.0.0.0/8"]

findings.title: Internet-facing Ingress has no authentication or rate limiting
findings.description: Ingress shop/storefront-ingress is exposed to the internet with no ingress-level authentication and no rate limit. Whether that is acceptable depends on whether the backend authenticates -- but the absence of a rate limit is unconditionally a denial of service and credential-stuffing exposure.

remediation.summary: Add rate limiting at the ingress; add edge authentication for non-public endpoints.
remediation.patch:
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "20"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "10"
    # for internal tools:
    # nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url: "https://oauth2-proxy.example.com/oauth2/auth"

findings.description: aws_instance worker allows IMDSv1. An SSRF in any application on the instance reaches 169.254.169.254 with a single unauthenticated GET and returns the instance role's temporary credentials. IMDSv2's PUT-token requirement blocks the entire SSRF class.

findings.title: Image runs as root
findings.description: The final stage of DockerImage node:latest has no USER instruction, so the image runs as UID 0. Every downstream consumer inherits that default -- an orchestrator has to opt out explicitly, and most manifests never do.

evidence.description: no USER instruction in the final stage

remediation.summary: Create and switch to a non-root user.
remediation.patch:
RUN addgroup -g 10001 app && adduser -D -u 10001 -G app app
USER 10001:10001

findings.title: Sensitive data crosses a trust boundary
findings.description: Deployment shop/storefront -> ExternalEntity Stripe (payment provider) moves data classified as pci across a trust boundary. Each boundary crossing is a place where authentication, authorisation, encryption, and logging all need to be re-established -- assumptions that held on one side rarely hold on the other.

remediation.summary: Enforce mTLS and explicit authorisation on this hop; log both sides.
remediation.guidance: A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) gives mTLS and per-hop authorisation policy without application changes, and produces the flow-level telemetry you need to detect abuse of this path.

findings.title: Container root filesystem is writable
findings.description: A writable root filesystem lets an attacker with code execution drop a web shell, overwrite application binaries, or install persistence that survives a process restart. It also removes a cheap tripwire: with a read-only root, most post-exploitation tooling fails immediately and noisily.

remediation.summary: Make the root filesystem read-only and mount emptyDir for writable paths.
remediation.patch:
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
# volumes:
#   - name: tmp
#     emptyDir: {}

notes: Reachable from the internet in 3 hops.

findings.title: Container image uses a mutable tag
findings.description: Container shop/web references image `shop/storefront:latest` by a mutable tag. What runs in production is therefore whatever the registry served at pull time. This breaks reproducibility, defeats admission-time image scanning, and makes supply chain tampering hard to detect -- an attacker who can push to the registry can replace the image without any manifest change.

remediation.summary: Pin images by digest.
remediation.patch:
image: myrepo/myapp@sha256:0f6a...   # digest, not :latest
imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

findings.title: Container has no CPU or memory limits
findings.description: Without resource limits, Container shop/web can consume all allocatable CPU and memory on its node. A memory leak or a deliberately expensive request becomes a node-wide outage: the kubelet begins evicting neighbouring pods, and a single compromised workload becomes a cluster-wide denial of service primitive.

remediation.summary: Set requests and limits; enforce defaults with a LimitRange.

findings.title: Pod does not set a seccomp profile
findings.description: No seccomp profile is applied, so the container may issue all ~350 syscalls. Most container escapes published in the last several years relied on syscalls that RuntimeDefault blocks outright.

remediation.summary: Apply the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile.
remediation.patch:
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault

findings.title: Workload uses the default service account
findings.description: Deployment shop/storefront runs as the namespace `default` service account with its token automounted. The default SA is shared by every workload in the namespace, so any permission granted to it is granted to all of them, and token theft cannot be attributed to a specific workload.

remediation.summary: Create a dedicated ServiceAccount per workload; disable automount if the API is not used.
remediation.patch:
spec:
  serviceAccountName: myapp
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # if the pod never calls the API server

findings.title: Container binds a host port
findings.description: Container shop/web binds host port(s) 8080. The service is reachable on every node IP, bypassing Service-level controls and NetworkPolicy, and it constrains scheduling in ways that make node-level firewalling brittle.

remediation.summary: Expose through a Service and an Ingress instead of a host port.

notes: Reachable from the internet in 3 hops.

findings.title: Workload has no egress NetworkPolicy
findings.description: Deployment shop/storefront has unrestricted egress. That is the exfiltration path and the command-and-control path: a compromised pod can reach any external host, any internal service, and the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254 to steal node IAM credentials.

remediation.summary: Default-deny egress; allow DNS plus the specific destinations required.
remediation.patch:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
  namespace: {{ namespace }}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except: ["169.254.169.254/32", "10.0.0.0/8"]

notes: Reachable from the internet in 2 hops.

findings.title: Service account token automounted on the default service account
findings.description: The `default` ServiceAccount in namespace shop automounts its token into every pod that does not specify another SA. This is the most commonly abused foothold for lateral movement inside a namespace.

remediation.summary: Disable automount on the default service account.
remediation.patch:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: {{ namespace }}
automountServiceAccountToken: false

findings.title: Security group allows ingress from 0.0.0.0/0
findings.description: aws_security_group web permits inbound traffic from the entire internet on port(s) 22. If any of those are 22, 3389, 3306, 5432, or 6379 this is immediately exploitable; even for 443 it removes the option of IP-based containment during an incident.

remediation.summary: Restrict to known CIDRs, or front the service with a load balancer and WAF.

findings.title: Data store has encryption at rest disabled
findings.description: aws_db_instance shop stores data unencrypted at rest. Snapshot sharing, disk decommissioning, and support access all become disclosure paths, and most compliance regimes treat this as a reportable control failure on its own.

remediation.summary: Enable encryption with a customer-managed KMS key.
remediation.patch:
storage_encrypted = true
kms_key_id        = aws_kms_key.data.arn

findings.title: Credential-like values stored in a ConfigMap
findings.description: ConfigMap shop/shop-config holds keys API_TOKEN that look like credentials. ConfigMaps get none of the (already modest) protections Secrets receive: they are not candidates for encryption at rest by default, are routinely granted broad read access, and are frequently dumped wholesale into logs and support bundles.

remediation.summary: Move these keys into a Secret or an external secret store, and rotate them.

findings.title: Remote content fetched with ADD
findings.description: ADD with a URL downloads and unpacks remote content with no integrity check. If the upstream host is compromised or DNS is hijacked, arbitrary content lands in the image at build time -- a textbook supply chain injection point.

remediation.summary: Download explicitly and verify a checksum or signature.
remediation.patch:
RUN curl -fsSLO https://example.com/tool.tar.gz \
 && echo "e3b0c442...  tool.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c - \
 && tar -xzf tool.tar.gz && rm tool.tar.gz

findings.title: Database deletion protection and final snapshot are both disabled
findings.description: aws_db_instance shop can be destroyed with no snapshot retained. A compromised CI credential, or a plain mistake in a `terraform apply`, results in unrecoverable data loss -- this is the destructive end of the availability spectrum.

remediation.summary: Enable deletion protection and keep final snapshots.

findings.title: Image has no HEALTHCHECK
findings.description: Without a HEALTHCHECK, a container that has hung but not exited is indistinguishable from a healthy one outside Kubernetes (where probes cover this).

remediation.summary: Add a HEALTHCHECK.

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/healthz || exit 1

findings.title: Service account token automounted but unused API access

findings.title: Namespace has no Pod Security Admission enforcement
findings.description: Namespace shop sets no pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label. Nothing prevents someone deploying a privileged, host-mounting pod here tomorrow, which means every workload-level fix in this report can be silently undone.

remediation.summary: Label the namespace with a Pod Security Standard.
remediation.patch:
metadata:
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted

findings.title: Namespace has no ResourceQuota
findings.description: Namespace shop has no ResourceQuota, so a single runaway or malicious workload here can consume the cluster's entire allocatable capacity and starve every other tenant.

evidence.description: no ResourceQuota found for this namespace

remediation.summary: Add a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange with sane defaults.
remediation.patch:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: {name: default-quota, namespace: {{ name }}}
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 40Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    limits.memory: 80Gi
    pods: "100"
